explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Verse 33 says he rented the vineyard out to some tenants and "…went away on a journey." No lawn chair by the wall, no binoculars in the tower. He handed over the keys and left.

That's right, baker. The landowner rented it out to the tenants and "…went away on a journey." He didn't hang around the vineyard watching them work. Renting it out and leaving is how the parable starts.

explanations.answer: To collect his share of the fruit
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Verse 34 says that when harvest time drew near, he sent his servants to collect his share of the fruit. It's his vineyard, so the fruit has an owner. The servants are there for the share and nothing else.

explanations.answer: To help bring in the harvest
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, friend, since harvest is busy work. But the text says the servants went to collect his share of the fruit. Nothing in the verse sends them to pick. They came for the share.

explanations.answer: To check on the wall and tower
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since the wall and tower were right there in verse 33. But verse 34 gives the reason for the visit: the servants were sent to collect his share of the fruit. The landowner didn't send them to inspect anything. They came for the fruit.

explanations.answer: Sends more servants than the first group
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Verse 36 says he sent other servants, more than the first group. Then the tenants did the same to them. Sending a bigger group after what just happened? I'd have sent a strongly worded letter, and that's about it.
That's a reasonable thing to picture, friend. But the text never mentions soldiers. Verse 36 says he sent other servants, more than the first group. The next move is another round of servants.

explanations.answer: Gives up on his share of the fruit
explanations.explanation: Not in this story, baker. After the servants were beaten, killed and stoned, verse 36 says he sent other servants again, and more of them this time. He's still sending people for what's owed. Whatever he's thinking, giving up isn't what the verse shows.
Yes, baker. Verse 37 says, "Finally, he sent his son to them." After the servants, the landowner sends his son. I think that tells you something about where this story is headed.
Close family, friend, but not the one in the text. Verse 37 says the landowner sent his son. No brother shows up anywhere in this parable.
A steward sounds official, I'll give you that. But no steward appears in this parable. Verse 37 says he sent his son. The last one he sends is family.

Right, baker. When he sends his son, he says, "They will respect my son…" (Matthew 21:37). That's the landowner's own hope as the son goes. So True is the answer, and the words come straight from him. Hold onto that line, because the very next verse is where it gets rough.
The text says otherwise, friend. In verse 37 the landowner says, ‘They will respect my son.’ That's what he says as he sends him. What the tenants do next is a different story.

That's it, baker. The tenants say, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance.’ They see the heir and go straight to the inheritance. I think this is a heavy part of the parable.
No robe in this story, friend. In verse 38 the tenants say, 'This is the heir,' and say they want to take his inheritance. The inheritance is what they name, not clothes.

A ring is a fun guess, but this parable never mentions one. The tenants say, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance.’ This is a heavy moment, and what they want is the inheritance.

explanations.answer: Bring them to a wretched end and rent to others
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Verse 41 has them saying, "He will bring those wretches to a wretched end…" and that he "…will rent out the vineyard to other tenants…" They answered Jesus' question themselves. I think they'd say it a little quieter if they knew where He was going with it.

explanations.answer: Forgive them and let them keep the vineyard
explanations.explanation: Forgiveness is a nice thought, friend, but it's not what they say. In verse 41 the listeners answer, "He will bring those wretches to a wretched end…" The vineyard goes to other tenants.

explanations.answer: Sell the vineyard and never come back
explanations.explanation: Interesting plan, but nobody says it. In verse 41 the listeners say the owner will bring those wretches to a wretched end. Then he will rent out the vineyard to other tenants, so the vineyard stays a vineyard.

Not quite, baker. In verse 41 the listeners say the new tenants will give the owner "…his share of the fruit at harvest time." The new tenants hand over his share, which is exactly what the first ones refused to do.

Right, baker. In verse 41 the listeners say the other tenants "…will give him his share of the fruit at harvest time." That's the very thing the first tenants wouldn't do. Think of a cookie swap where somebody actually brings cookies.

Yes, baker! Jesus quotes, "The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone." (Psalm 118:22; Matthew 21:42). The builders rejected it, and it ends up as the cornerstone. That's quite a turn for one stone.

That's not how the line goes, friend. Jesus quotes, "The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone." (Psalm 118:22; Matthew 21:42). The line says the builders rejected the stone, and it has become the cornerstone. Being carried away isn't in it.

explanations.answer: It gets left in the field
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since this whole parable happens around a vineyard. But the line Jesus quotes says, "The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone." (Psalm 118:22; Matthew 21:42). No field in that one. The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone.

That's right, baker. The Scripture says, "This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes…" (Psalm 118:23; Matthew 21:42). Both halves matter. It's from the Lord, and it's marvelous in our eyes.
Actually the Scripture says it is. Jesus quotes, "This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes…" (Psalm 118:23; Matthew 21:42). The stone becoming the cornerstone is from the Lord.

explanations.answer: A people who will produce its fruit
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says the kingdom of God "…will be taken away from you and given to a people who will produce its fruit." The kingdom goes to people who produce fruit. Same word the whole parable has been using.

explanations.answer: The servants who were sent first
explanations.explanation: I see the thinking, friend, since those servants had a rough time. But verse 43 doesn't name them. Jesus says it will be given to "…a people who will produce its fruit."

explanations.answer: The builders who rejected the stone
explanations.explanation: That one flips the verse around, baker. The builders are the ones who rejected the stone in the Scripture Jesus quotes. In verse 43 He says the kingdom will be given to "…a people who will produce its fruit."

Yes, baker. Verse 45 says the chief priests and Pharisees "…knew that Jesus was speaking about them." They heard the parables and figured it out. When a story lands that close, nobody has to explain it.

explanations.answer: Jesus is speaking about the crowds
explanations.explanation: Close to the right scene, friend, but not the right people. Verse 45 says the chief priests and Pharisees knew Jesus was speaking about them. The crowds come up in the next verse, and it's a different matter there.

explanations.answer: Jesus is speaking about tax collectors
explanations.explanation: Tax collectors aren't in this scene, baker. Verse 45 says the chief priests and Pharisees knew Jesus was speaking about them. They heard the parables and understood who they were about.
Right, baker. Verse 46 says they wanted to arrest Him but were afraid of the crowds. So a want and a fear sit in the same verse. The crowds are the fear the text names.
That's right. Verse 46 says the people regarded Him as a prophet. The chief priests and Pharisees wanted to arrest Him, but the crowds held that view of Him. That's why they held back.
No soldiers in this verse, friend. Verse 46 says they were afraid of the crowds. Soldiers aren't mentioned there, and the crowds are what the text says they feared.
Good guess with the temple setting, but the verse says something else. In verse 46 the people regarded Jesus as a prophet. Priest isn't the word the text uses.
There's no governor in this passage, baker. Verse 46 says the chief priests and Pharisees were afraid of the crowds. And the people regarded Jesus as a prophet. Not a governor, that's for sure.
